title: Uber Cuts Translation Cache Memory by up to 90% While Keeping P99 Latency Below 1 MS
gist: Uber redesigned its Go translation cache into a hybrid memory/disk design (all keys in memory, values in 256 disk-backed shards with LRU and access-history preload), cutting initial memory footprint by over 90% while keeping p99 miss latency under 1 ms and hit rate above 99.9%, after first cutting GC overhead by replacing sync.Map.

insights.claim: Memory profiling across Uber's Go services found garbage collection consuming more than 20% of CPU in some services, with translation entries accounting for about 70% of allocated objects.
insights.speaker: Leela Kumili
insights.so_what: Shows how hidden GC costs in managed-language services translate into material compute spend at hyperscale.

insights.claim: Replacing Go's sync.Map with a plain map[string]string guarded by an RWMutex for a read-heavy, rarely updated workload reduced pointer-heavy object allocations and improved CPU utilization by more than 30% in the affected Uber service.
insights.speaker: Leela Kumili
insights.so_what: Cheap data-structure changes can yield double-digit CPU savings; a signal that infra cost optimization still has low-hanging fruit.
insights.locator: The first optimization replaced Go's sync.Map

insights.claim: Uber's translation datasets held two to three million keys although individual services accessed only a small subset, and the background-build-then-atomic-swap refresh doubled memory during refreshes, causing some services to run out of memory.
insights.speaker: Leela Kumili
insights.so_what: Double-buffered cache refreshes are a common hidden driver of memory over-provisioning.
insights.locator: However, reducing object allocations did not solve

insights.claim: Uber rejected an external cache and per-service translation subsets due to operational and maintenance costs, instead keeping all keys in memory and moving values to disk behind the unchanged Get()/Put() API, using 256 shards each with its own RWMutex, six-byte hash keys with collision fallback, a time-based global LRU, and a preload of translations accessed in the prior 15 minutes on refresh.
insights.speaker: Leela Kumili
insights.so_what: A reusable pattern for cutting RAM costs where access is highly skewed, reducing need for external caches like Redis.

insights.claim: After Uber's cache redesign, a translation dataset that used about 800 MB in memory needed about 40 MB of metadata, with total memory typically 80-120 MB under a 50,000-entry in-memory limit; overall memory fell from roughly 2.7 GB to 750 MB.
insights.speaker: Leela Kumili
insights.so_what: Up to 90% memory reduction per service directly lowers fleet RAM requirements.
insights.locator: In one example, a translation dataset

insights.claim: In one Uber workload only about 30,000 of more than four million translation entries were held in memory while the hit rate stayed above 99.9% and p99 latency for disk-backed misses stayed below 100 microseconds.
insights.speaker: Leela Kumili
insights.so_what: Extreme access skew means most cached data need not sit in expensive RAM, a broader argument for tiered memory/storage.

insights.claim: Uber recommends minimizing object references to reduce GC overhead and measuring how often cached values are actually accessed, moving cold values to disk when only a small fraction of cached data is active.
insights.speaker: Leela Kumili
insights.so_what: Generalizable cost lever for any large in-memory caching fleet.
insights.quote: At Uber's scale, even small inefficiencies in memory management can add up.
insights.locator: Uber's experience highlights the cost implications
